utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Yes, Mr. Gaynor, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Poparic, when we broke yesterday we were discussing the measurement of the azimuth of the Markale 2 incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: If we call up --

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, but I cannot hear well. Can the volume be raised?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Somebody needs to speak for a test so I'll do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you hear me -- no? Let us see. Yes. Mr. Poparic, do you hear me well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay, okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Poparic.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, when we broke yesterday we were discussing the measurement of the azimuth of the Markale 2 incident, and if we can go, please, to your report D3644 at page 112 in English and that's 113 in B/C/S. Now if we could focus, please, on footnote 212. Yesterday you clarified your evidence about the measurements by the French UNPROFOR troops and you accepted that you had made a mistake in footnote 211. Now in footnote 212 you say: "It is clear that the French sappers did not measure the azimuth of 2850 mils and that for unknown reasons they accepted the results of the measurement of the Sarajevo CSB." Now, Mr. Poparic, is it correct that you now accept that the French did in fact measure the azimuth themselves?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will explain. I accept that they measured the azimuth - and that's the one we can see on the video-clip, that's the azimuth at 2.800, 157.5 degrees is the value - and they rounded up the value to 2.850 which is 165 degrees. It's interesting that the CSB also measured an azimuth of 2.850, but the units of measure are different. The CSB of Sarajevo has units where the circle is divided into 6.000 units, whereas the French divided into 6.400 units. These two facts make the results appear the same at first sight, but they differ substantially by 10 or 11 degrees. They did measure 2800 and rounded it up to 2850 which matches the other result, but different units were applied and there is a substantial difference in the azimuth --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Let's have a look at the report of CSB Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could we look at P1908, page 3, B/C/S, page 2 in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll not broadcast this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now in this report it's clear that the CSB Sarajevo have accorded the azimuth as 170 degrees plus or minus 5 degrees. It's in paragraph 2. There's no reference in that report to any measurement by mils. And also we can look at it in a minute, P1934 - perhaps we can look at it now - which is a report compiled by Emir Turkusic. And if we look at that at page 5 in B/C/S and page 4 in English, we see there that Emir Turkusic, who was also within the RBiH MUP but within the KDZ part of that measured it as 170 degrees plus or minus 5 degrees. So what is the basis of your assertion that the investigators of the Sarajevo CSB used a compass with a division of 1.600 while they did the calculation and what is the relevance of that assertion to these figures?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The CSB Sarajevo investigators worked together with UNMO observers, I believe. There was a Lieutenant-Colonel Konings. And in the report of the UNMO observers it is stated that the azimuth was 170 degrees or 2850 mils. In some documents that you showed, the value is expressed in degrees, but in some others it's expressed in mils. 170, according to this division of 1:6.000 is -- equals 2850 mils or actually a little less. The exact value is 170 point something. Now, in this system of a division of 6.000 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down and repeat the figures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Poparic, please speak slowly and repeat from: "The system of division of 6.000 ..."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If these 170 degrees are expressed in mils according to the division of the circle into 6.000, we'll get 2850 or -- actually, that's a bit over 170 but that can be neglected. If the value of 2850 in the division of 1:6400 is converted into degrees, then we get 165 degrees. That's the value the French sappers came up with. And the difference is about 10 degrees. There are documents here, though, that state the value as 170 degrees or 2850 mils. So there can be no error.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: But you accept that the French UNPROFOR troops recorded the value as 2.850 mils and the CSB recorded the value in degrees as 170 plus or minus 5 degrees; you accept that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I accept that the French measured the value of 2850. They put down 2850, but actually I heard that they measured 2800 which is not a significant error. That was fairly done. It's -- we're talking about a rounding of 2 degrees. And there's a police clip where we see that they're using military compasses that has a division into mils. Now, how they converted the values, I don't know. Maybe they measured the value in degrees originally and then converted into mils or the other way around, I don't know, but it doesn't really matter. I accept that this is the result of CSB and UNMO and this result equal -- is equal to an angle of 2850 mils in the 1:6.000 division. If it were -- we're talking about the 1:6400 division, then the value would be slightly different, about 3.000. And the difference is obvious and there can be no confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: All right. We'll move on to another subject. If we can turn to the next page in English and B/C/S of your report, which is D3644. That's page 113 in English and 114 in B/C/S. We're now going to look at your assertions concerning the cymbeline radar system. On that page you say that -- it goes: "On the condition that the shell had a certain minimum angle of descent of 67 degrees and considering the conditions for which the radar had been set up, it was easy to determine the maximum lower incoming trajectory for each charge ..." And if we turn to the next page in both languages, we see the graph containing a great deal of information about that Cymbeline radar. Now, did you draw this graph yourself?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mrs. Subotic and I drew it. These trajectories are -- were calculated using a programme used to make firing tables. We used it to have a graph with the relevant points, but it seems we failed to point out to which shell this is applied. It's the M49 shell which corresponds to the Russian 0F-473 model. We chose it deliberately, although I'm not sure that the VRS had these shells because the UNPROFOR report stating that these shells could not be seen on the radar is based on the firing table for this M49 shell, that's why we calculated the trajectories for this very shell to check what UNPROFOR had stated. And, by the way, the range of this shell is shorter than that of the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Can we focus, Mr. Registrar, on either one of these images. They're both exactly the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, you're confirming that these trajectories are not in fact for the 120-millimetre mortar projectile; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. We misunderstood each other. It's not 122 but 120. But these are the trajectories for a 120-millimetre mortar shell, but it's an older model that was manufactured under licence from the Russians. It is called a heavy shell and the one used now is a light shell. So this one is a bit heavier and has a shorter range and carries a bit more explosive and so on. That's why I pointed out that we calculated these trajectories for this very shell because the UNPROFOR in its report stated the limitations in range and explained why it couldn't be seen on the radar and all that referred to this mine. So there can be no mistake. In the report about the shelling, the trajectories for that other shell were stated, which actually corroborates what I'm saying. We have information for both kinds of shell showing that they couldn't be seen on the radar.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: But the trajectories we're looking at on the screen at the moment do not correspond to the trajectories for the MK -- M74, 120-millimetre mortar projectile which is considered to have been the cause of the explosion at Markale; is that right? That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll explain. It's that mortar that you mentioned, but it's not the M62 shell but the M48 -- sorry, M49 shell. It's only a different shell fired from the same mortar because one mortar can fire different types of shell. These are newer shells. The M62 shell is the most frequent model and there are other variants, whereas the older model is heavier. This is the shell for the 120-millimetre shell that was allegedly used to fire a shell on the Markale market.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 6, lines 5 and 6, due to the different rules applying to negations in Serbian and English, it was recorded wrongly. The witness said that it was impossible that they could not be seen on the radar. [In English] It showed that they couldn't be -- it couldn't be that they hadn't been seen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think I'm following.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 6, line 5, I'll read out what was recorded. [In English] It showed that they couldn't be seen on the radar. It should be all the way around. It couldn't happen that they wouldn't be seen on the radar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you see that, Mr. Gaynor? Line -- it's line 1.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Line 5, line 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: It's just slipped off my screen but we can -- I can ask the witness to clarify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Poparic, you heard that. Could you clarify what your words were.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that we showed that the M49 shell fired from a 120-millimetre mortar must have been caught by the radar beam, and we also showed in the other report containing a similar diagram that the M62 shell fired from the same mortar also must have been caught by the radar beam. All shells irrespective of the model fired from that mortar must have been caught by the radar beam. I think it's clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in any event your analysis depends to a very great deal on the location of the centre point of the radar beam and of the radius of that beam which was in operation on that day. So I want to explore that with you. And a third point which is the location of the centre point of the radar beam in comparison to the market-place. So let's start with the first thing. Do you see the centre point of the radar beam which appears to be quite high in the sky above the market-place? What is the source of your placing the centre point of the radar beam at that point?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The centre point you are referring to is irrelevant in this depiction of ours. The height of 548 metres - or we can round it to 550 - this line is important because that's what UNPROFOR stated as a -- for which UNPROFOR was a source, above which anything must have been caught, which means that a trajectory 900 metres high would not have been registered, whereas if we were to show the other diagram in the other report, it would be easier to explain. This height of 550 metres is the height of which UNPROFOR says that anything above that must have been observed. It was stated by the engineers using the radar. Maybe the radar beam was wider, but that is not important. We only made a sketch, an approximate sketch of the front of the radar beam in relation to the trajectory. It may have been twice as wide or half as wide, but that's not really relevant. All we care about is the lower limit because the problem is the lower limit and not the centre point.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sir, you're suggesting that two things are irrelevant. One is the centre point of the radar beam and the second is the radius of the radar beam; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right. It is relevant for the one who decides how to position the radar and how to -- where to point it, but I think they did a very good job about that because the report states that it was at about 1.050 metres from the separation line. I don't think that's precise enough because if we look at the situation on the ground the separation line was some 2 kilometres away. They probably had in mind the direction of the radar beam. Why was it necessary to place the radar there? It was their task to observe all the projectiles coming from the VRS positions and vice versa. If we take a look at Sarajevo, how wide the inhabited area is, then we're talking about some 4 to 5 kilometres. And if we consider the lower or the descending part of the trajectory, then ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Poparic --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat the last part of his sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you repeat the last part of your answer.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that Sarajevo is 4 to 5 kilometres wide there, and if we imagine that the furthest point is targeted or the point nearest to the VRS positions, then the radar must be positioned in such a way that it can catch all these trajectories. And this position of a thousand metres is roughly at the point where all the trajectories meet, as is the case here. They would all be within the beam. And the technicians who did that did a very good job about positioning their radar.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Poparic, at the bottom of -- just under this graph in the English language version you say: "It can be seen in the picture that there was no curve which could have slipped under the beam ..." Now, I put it to you surely that depends on exactly where the centre point of the radar beam was and how large the radius of the radar beam was on the day in question?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I believe that this has been misinterpreted because it says here that it could not go under the beam, which means that they all had to be caught within the beam. That's the essence. In principle you are right. It depends on the central point of the radar beam and its width. However, we did not have that information. We received a different piece of information. According to the information that we received, we got the lower limit of the radar beam which was 548 or 550. That was the most important thing for us. Everything above that would go beyond the radar beam, you see. What matters to us is the lower limit, and we received that information from the UNPROFOR report. And this is official data.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Poparic, thank you for confirming that you did not have information on the central point of the radar beam and its width. I'd like you also to confirm that you do not have any information for where precisely the radar was located in relation to the target or in relation to the front line; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is some information as to its position, but we don't have the exact co-ordinates.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat once again, we received the official UNPROFOR data from its report about the height at which the radar could not caught any of the trajectories, and this is the only relevant information. The rest is technical details which matter to the people who placed the radar and handled the radar, who make sure that the radar beam catches everything. In our report, it is stated what was the minimum height up to which the trajectories could be caught. We received that from UNPROFOR. And let me repeat: Based on that they concluded that they -- the trajectory slipped under the beam. We are showing here that UNPROFOR when it claims that the radar beam which caught trajectories up to 550 metres could not catch these trajectories. However, we demonstrate very clear that it was supposed to all -- to catch all the trajectories, so we have to compare what UNPROFOR claimed and what was the real situation on the ground.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And if you show that part in the shelling report, I can provide some more details as to where UNPROFOR made a cardinal mistake in their analysis and this is the key to the whole problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 10, line 9 and 10, we again have a countersense. It says: [In English] "... that would go beyond the radar beam, you see." [Interpretation] The witness said that everything that would go above 548 would have been registered by the radar because it would have been caught by the radar beam.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this is what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Poparic, ultimately you are asking the Trial Chamber to prefer your graph and your conclusions over the conclusions reached by UNPROFOR, which was the organisation which was actually operating the radar on the day of the Markale incident; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not asking for anything from the Trial Chamber, I don't have that right. I'm just telling you what the situation was. The fact is, however, that UNPROFOR operated the radar and that they claim that the radar was on for 24 hours, that it was in a good working order. The fact is also that none of the technicians who operated the radar confirmed the findings that the radar could not catch any of the shells. The conclusion was reached by Lieutenant-Colonel Powers [phoen] together with General Smith. I don't know whether he is an artillery man or something else. However, none of the technicians who were in charge of operating the radar didn't -- confirmed the finding that the radar beam was placed in such a way that it could not catch those trajectories. We claim that it would have been impossible if we bear in mind that -- the position of the radar beam. The key issue here is the height, the lowest level of the radar beam, of 548 or 550 metres if we round it off.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: We'll move now to the Markale 1 incident which is the next incident -- actually, it appears at page 116 in the English of your report. You have there a graph setting out the possibility of hitting the target with the first shot. Now, let's just go through this graph in some detail. First of all, the target dimensions of 25.8 metres by 34 metres, that refers to your understanding of the size of the Markale market-place; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's how large the market is, and you can see it on the land survey map that we had at our disposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Very good. Now, if we can just go to charge 0 plus 5 as an example, we see that the Vd set out is 29 metres and the Vp is 12 metres. Now, if we can translate that into layman's language, that essentially means that if you were to fire a 120-millimetre mortar projectile from a distance of 5.782 metres from the market-place, there is a 50 per cent chance that it would land within an ellipse which is 58 metres by 24 metres. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that you are wrong in just one thing. When you use this Vd and Vp, when we are talking about probable deviations on range and on direction and when we say 50 per cent of the hits will be correct, this concerns a group of projectiles. If we fired ten of them, we can expect that five will hit the target. If ten are fired, it may be expected that five will hit the target, and we're talking about a different thing here. In the theory of firing, it is also studied and the calculations are based on that at theory. We are looking for the information as to how probable it is for the shell -- the first shell to be correct because we had only one shell here. In the theory of firing, we have a solution to that problem as well. What is the probability for the first shell to hit your target? And this is not the same as when you have a group of projectiles because the first five may be off target, the last five may hit the target, so you get your 50 per cent. Here the issue is how probable is it for the first projectile to hit the target? And this is a different matter. So we're talking about a very essential difference in looking at the probability through the Vd and Vp statistical measures because we're talking about a group of projectiles. We're not talking about a sequence of projectiles that will hit the target. We say if there is ten of them, we have a 50 per cent probability that they will hit the target, which means five will hit the target and five will be off target. According to the theory of firing, there is also a probability which we have to calculate, and that is how probable is it that the first projectile would hit the target. The probability is much lower and it is only logical.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, can we move to the next page of your report, please, and there we have a sketch which has been prepared, I understand, either by you or Mrs. Subotic of what you understand to be the dimensions of Markale market-place. And if we can focus in just on the sketch. First of all, can you confirm as a separate issue that the placement of the stalls in this sketch that you prepared is not, in fact, based on the contemporaneous video taken in the minutes after the incident?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A few minutes after the incident the stalls were all over the place. There is a difference. This is the placement which differs in the passage between Marsal Tito Street and Dzenetica Cikma Street. On the day of the incident in that area there were more stalls in the -- that passage, approximately up to here, up to the building on 22nd December. There are two -- there were two rows of stalls, and there was an obstacle in the passage from Marsal Tito to Dzenetica Cikma Street with stalls -- you couldn't go through that passage. I don't know why. Later on on the clip you can see that they were moving those stalls and then you can see the cars entering that area in order to transport the dead. On the day of the incident that area was full of stalls for some unknown reason. But this is an approximate layout, this is a schematic representation of the layout. But when we are talking about the probability, that probability referred to the entire market. We looked at the probability for the shell to hit the entire area, and if we had looked at the probability of the shell hitting anywhere between any of the stalls, the calculation would be totally different.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, I want to take you to --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On line 18 and 19, the witness said -- it says: [In English] "A few minutes after the incident the stalls were all over the place." [Interpretation] The witness said the stalls were upside down. Everything was [In English] Turned over or turned upside down [Interpretation] Overturned or turned upside down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Do you confirm that, Mr. Poparic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can confirm, but I would like to also to emphasise that the main difference between the sketch and the real situation in the market-place lies in the fact that I mentioned a while ago. In the passage between Marsal Tito street and Dzenetica Cikma Street there were another longitudinal row of stalls and there were also some stalls that prevented the passage into that street for some unknown reasons and those stalls were perpendicular to the row of longitudinal stalls.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So in the end you agree with Mr. Gaynor that this is not based upon the contemporaneous scene? That was the crux of the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we are looking at the number of the stalls and their layout, Mr. Gaynor is right. As far as the dimensions of the market-place are concerned, this is correct. This sketch was transferred from the land survey map. It is very precise. We checked that it tallies with the real situation. The dimension of the market-place correspond to the situation as it was on the day, and as for the layout of the stalls, it may have been different but we did not even take that into consideration when we were calculating our probabilities. All we were looking at was the area, the space of the market-place.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Poparic, we'll take it for the purposes of this exercise that we accept the dimensions of the market-place itself are correct, setting aside any difference we might have about the location of the stalls. And I'd like the usher to assist you with a pen and I'd like you to draw an ellipse in whatever direction you prefer of 24 metres by 58 metres around that market-place, please.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be correct to start at the centre of the market. If somebody were to target it, obviously it would be logical for that person to choose -- I will assume that it is here. What did we say? 24 --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You say that the market-place was 25.8 metres by 34 metres. And I'd like you to draw an ellipse of 24 metres by 58 metres.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The axis or semi-axis should be 24 or -- I didn't understand you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I would like you to draw around the market-place an ellipse of 24 metres by 58 metres.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So the entire ellipse should be 24? Is that what you're asking me to do?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Poparic, you know exactly what I'm asking you to do.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether we understood each other properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You know what an ellipse is, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know, yes. When I draw an ellipse, we usually use semi-axes. Are you referring to the external dimensions of the ellipse? Okay. 24 by 58 -- okay. I will draw based on what I understood. This could be it if we understood each other well, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I think we have. Now, that marks the area within which 50 per cent of the projectiles would land if you were to fire a 120-millimetre mortar projectile from a distance of 5.782 metres from the market-place; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right, but if we are talking about a group of projectiles, if several projectiles are fired. This is only logical. If we say that the probability is 50, that means if ten projectiles were fired it is to be expected that five will land in this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Well, I put it to you that the mortar crew which had fired this projectile in fact stood a pretty good chance of hitting the market-place if they wanted to, especially if they were firing from a mortar which had been in position for many months and they had access to prerecorded target data.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This doesn't change anything in the conclusion, what we're talking about. And these are Vd and Vp. These are not only characteristics of the mortar. It also means that we're talking about the characteristics of the shell as well, and it all depends on the crew. They cannot influence the characteristics that a shell has. It is a projectile which has some shortcomings and there is also a dispersion that you have to take into account. And it's not up to the crew. The crew can calculate the elements, it can do its job well, it can position the asset properly, so -- so as to increase the precision. But the Vd and the Vp that we're talking about are the characteristics of the shell and there -- nobody can influence that. Every shell will have a dispersion margin that the crew cannot influence. The crew can perhaps increase that dispersion if they do not have the firm basis for the asset and they don't calculate the elements properly. Every shell has some shortcomings which reflect in the lack of precision which can be bigger or smaller. And this is implied by Vd and Vp. These are characteristics of the series of the ammunition. When you test ammunition, the criteria that is applied is whether that shell satisfies the criterion of probable dispersion. This is the characteristics that are characteristic of ammunition on which a crew cannot influence. I heard somebody -- a member of the crew who said: I can hit a match, which is ridiculous. No person can influence the characteristics of ammunition. Vd and Vp are primarily the characteristics of a shell and the crew cannot influence that. You also have to take into account weather conditions, the wind, and everything else, and all that falls under the general category of Vd and Vp.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you sign --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, while witness signs this image. Yes, Mr. Karadzic. Just a second. Be careful. Let's not lose your marking. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now this has been clarified; however, on line 4 there is again a countersense. The witness sense that this doesn't at all depend on the crew.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Of crew at all, not all depends.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'd like to tender that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll admit this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6349, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. President, no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Shall we have a short break, five minutes, to change the setting? We'll continue with Mr. Kecmanovic. Correct? Yes. You understand the schedule, Mr. Poparic? You heard the -- there's a change in the witness schedule, so your evidence will be interposed by Mr. Kecmanovic's evidence. I thank you for your kind understanding, Mr. Poparic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: And just to be clear, Mr. President, Mr. Poparic is to remain in the building because we expect to resume his evidence later today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Five minutes. --- Break taken at 9.52 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would the witness make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kecmanovic. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good morning, Excellencies. Good morning to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Professor Kecmanovic. Did you hear me?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Tell us, did you give a statement to my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And thank you for making a pause before answering and speaking slowly so that the transcript may be accurate.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now call up in e-court 1D7351.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see on the screen in front of you your statement?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you read and sign this statement?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we show the last page so that Mr. Kecmanovic may identify his signature.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this statement faithfully reflect what you said to my Defence team and is there some sort of confusion concerning an abbreviation, or rather, does it faithfully reflect what you said and disregard what I said last because it relates to the English version only?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I were to put the same questions to you today would your answers essentially be the same?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, essentially they would.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us, what would be the abbreviation in Serbian for the party that you headed in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: SRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Meaning? What is the full name?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: The Alliance of Reform Forces of Yugoslavia for Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does the abbreviation in Serbian call to mind some other political parties and are there any connections there?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The acronym is the same as that for the Serbian Radical Party. Now, the orientation of my party was pro-Yugoslav. It was a party in Bosnia-Herzegovina and I was the leader of that party in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And the then-prime minister Ante Markovic was the leader of the party at the level of Yugoslavia. Now, because of our orientation some members of other political parties would half jokingly/half seriously say that we were the party of reserve Serbs. The reformist orientation was how they referred to us because we were in favour of remaining in Yugoslavia but that was also the orientation of the Serbian Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I wish to tender this document into evidence, but I only wish to note that the acronym of SRS in it does not stand - and I mean in the English version - does not stand for the Serbian Radical Party but rather for the Alliance of Reform Forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. In the English version it's noted as SRSJ.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Karadzic is actually referring to paragraph 8, where there is the "Serbian Radical Party" behind the abbreviation "SRS" and that's wrong.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that it was in the course of translation that this came about. This was an interpretation on the part of the translator that this was the Serbian Radical Party, and I wish to thank my learned friend for this comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Noted. Any objection, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: However, in the view of the Chamber paragraphs 45 and 46 of Mr. Kecmanovic's statement contain a detailed information about mistreatment of Bosnian Serbs, including the existence of detention centres. The Chamber is of the view that this level of detail is not relevant to the charges against the accused, and accordingly orders the redaction of these paragraphs. With that redaction, the Chamber will admit Mr. Kecmanovic's statement as Defence -- next Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3645, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will now read Professor Dr. Nenad Kecmanovic's statement in a summary version in English and then I will put some other questions. [In English] Nenad Kecmanovic was president of the Alliance of Reform Forces of Yugoslavia for BH. Until 1989 he was a member of the Communist Party. He was nominated as BH representative for a member of the SFRY Presidency. After the elections of 1990, the Assembly of the Bosnia and Herzegovina was accepted positively by the public. On June the 1st of 1992, Professor Kecmanovic joined the BH Presidency. He proposed a work programme to be established within the BH Presidency. Alija Izetbegovic was the only one who kept reservations against the platform which was based on the Cutileiro Plan. Communication with the other parts of BH was not possible for all members of the Presidency except for Alija Izetbegovic. In April 1992, Professor Kecmanovic participated in a meeting with Mirko Pejanovic, Momcilo Krajisnik, and Radovan Karadzic at Terme hotel in Ilidza where specific measures to deal with the situation of conflicts were discussed. A subsequent meeting with the same purpose was arranged in May 1992 between Momcilo Krajisnik and Alija Izetbegovic. Momcilo Krajisnik proposed temporary division of the territory according to the existing territorial and ethnic distribution and the front line. Pressure came from the Serbian people because there were victims falling on both sides. A copy of this plan was also sent to Pale. In spring 1992, the status of the BH -- of the JNA in BH was discussed by the Yugoslav President Branko Kostic and Minister of Defence General Adzic. A proposal for an agreement was accepted and supported by Slobodan Milosevic; however, it was rejected within the BH Presidency. The JNA was supposed to remain in BH to guarantee peace and security and to prevent inter-ethnic conflicts. President Karadzic was fully concerned about what was happening in Sarajevo. The National Equality Council was developed before the elections in 1990. Its primary functions were to ensure the protection of vital national interests of each of the three constituent peoples and to preserve the equality of the rights of all ethnic groups. Out-voting of the Serbian deputies in the BH Assembly was one of the main causes of the war. Between the end of 1991 and March 1992, the situation in the entire country was especially in Sarajevo very tense and violence kept spreading. Attacks were mainly carried out against the Serbs, especially against the families of the JNA officers. The Serbian side launched an initiative to enable citizens of Sarajevo to leave the city if they wished, supported also by President Karadzic. Regardless of their ethnicity, the Serbian side guaranteed everyone safe passage across its territory. After May 1992, it was impossible to leave Sarajevo. The media espoused war time propaganda: The Muslim victims were innocent and crimes were committed only by the Serbian army. Private prisons in Sarajevo exclusively detained Serbian civilians and abused them under false accusations that they were hiding weapons or giving light signals to the Serbian artillery. For example, they existed in the basement of the Zagreb hotel, those prisons, and Europa hotel. The police organs, including Minister Delimustafic, had no information about this and could not assist in freeing these people. During meetings with leading representatives of the Serbian leadership in summer of 1992, the shelling of Sarajevo was raised on several occasions. The shelling was arbitrary and non-selective as presented. The Muslim artillery was located in the most densely populated parts in the city and Serbian artillery was forced to respond to the fire aiming towards the locations where the fire was coming from. As to how the events were reported through media, news came from two sides: Radio Sarajevo, which was under Muslim control, and Radio SRNA under Serbian control. BBC and other global media transmitted information similar to the one provided by the Muslim media. That had quite a substantial effect on Muslims and Croats, who in the beginning kept the same distance from all three ethnic parties. Later, they became negatively biased against the SDS, RS, and the Serbs. President Karadzic emphasised the necessity to find a solution for the conflict in BH through political negotiations and to avoid or stop the war at any cost. [Interpretation] That would be the short summary. I'd like to put several additional questions to Professor Kecmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Firstly, not challenging the ruling of the Trial Chamber concerning paragraphs 55 and 56, your decision to leave Sarajevo, did it have anything to do with the elements related in these paragraphs? In other words, was it what you could or could not do for the citizens of Sarajevo of other ethnicities something that had an impact on this decision of yours?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Of course, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, that's just blatantly leading and not -- and I will stop there. You could have asked: What's the reason for your leaving? Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, that's actually also the objection and proposal I would have made, but I also want to note that he also in the summary did disregard your decision and has basically exactly told these details that you had just excluded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, back to you, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. But it was excluded only today. Had it been excluded earlier on, I would have left it out of the summary. But at any rate, the summary is not an exhibit so no prejudice there or no damage there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Professor Kecmanovic, did you have an opportunity to become familiar with the SDA policy vis-a-vis the multi-ethnic character of Bosnia and their espousal of a civic state? What was it that you observed during your political work and especially during your tenure in the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: The political activity of the Party of Democratic Action - at the time, Muslim; today, Bosniak - consisted of a contradiction, as it were, which emerged sometime in the watershed period when the US Ambassador Zimmerman and Izetbegovic met which was during the Lisbon negotiations under the leadership or chairmanship of Cutileiro. Up until that point, the Party of Democratic Action mostly operated as a counterpart to the SDS and HDZ. It had a national agenda and was mono-ethnic by composition. I think it also had the elements of a religious party. This especially applied to Izetbegovic, the leader of the party, and his closer associates who were put on trial in the so-called Sarajevo trial because of Islamic -- Muslim fundamentalism. And let me say that the SDA was the first one to be set up as a national party, followed by the HDZ and then SDS, within two months of each other. So from a purely national or religious national party, it underwent a sudden change of turn where it was all of a sudden advocating a civic Bosnian state. So this was a turnabout which was supposed to camouflage what was a strategic change where Bosnia and Herzegovina would be a state ruled by the three parties that won the elections, but in this way suddenly it would become a unitary state led by the predominant force which was at the time the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'd like to add and say that the -- had the Bosniak population wanted this unitary option, they would not have voted for the SDA but rather for my party, the Party of Reform Forces or the late Nijaz Durakovic's party. And there was several more parties who had this multi-ethnic character because they gathered representatives of all the three ethnicities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So can you tell us how many of these multi-ethnic parties were there that you just referred to?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there was the party that I headed at the level of Bosnia-Herzegovina, this is the Alliance of Reform Forces of Yugoslavia for Bosnia-Herzegovina; there was the SDP, which was practically the reformed communist party or the League of Communists as they used to be called; then there was the liberal civic party led by Rasim Kadic; there was also a party of civic orientation, although it was composed primarily of Bosniak Muslims, that's Zulfikarpasic, the party of Adil Zulfikarpasic, a Muslim-Bosniak party as it was called, which unlike the SDA advocated that there -- that an agreement be reached with the Serbs and Croats. It was in favour of Bosnia-Herzegovina remaining within Yugoslavia. It was a party which had an inner circle of Bosniak elite with a pro-civic orientation. Adil Zulfikarpasic himself had lived for a long time abroad in Switzerland and returned to Sarajevo shortly before the war. It seemed to me that he espoused similar ideas and similar activities shortly before the elections, and I mean political party activities. There was a period of time where Zulfikarpasic appeared together with Izetbegovic; however, it was precisely on the issues that I mentioned earlier on that they parted ways because Zulfikarpasic thought that the SDA espoused extremist views. In some of his books that were published he even referred to it as a fascist or a pro-fascist party. That was where his confrontation with Izetbegovic emerged. And at a meeting in Tesanj which was one of the main strongholds of the SDA, because of these positions up there, they were excommunicated from the SDA, and that was when he proceeded to establish this Muslim-Bosniak party of his.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did Mr. Pejanovic also have a party of his own? I think you mentioned him somewhere.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Pejanovic headed the socialist party as it was called, just as the SDP was a transformed League of Communists, Pejanovic headed the socialist party which was a reformed socialist alliance. For those who are less well-versed with it, before the war in the socialist Yugoslavia this was an organisation akin to a national front. It was there to gather the broad national masses who favoured socialism but were not communists.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since foreigners find it difficult to tell somebody's ethnicity on the basis of their name, can you tell us out of these five alternative multi-ethnic parties had Muslim leaders and how many had other leaders?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, Pejanovic was a Serb, just as I am; Zulfikarpasic was undoubtedly a Muslim, a Bosniak, was - he passed away; as for the Liberal Civic Party, it was led by Rasim Kadic, who was also a Muslim or a Bosniak. Those were the more important parties. I can't recall others.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And later Durakovic?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was the head of the SDP, the Reformed Communists, also a Bosniak, Muslim, passed away recently.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us if you were privy to the war strategy of the Presidency or the Muslim part of it with regard to interventions of a foreign military force. Were you able to learn anything about their position on this score?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, primarily what could be observed and heard in the Presidency in the span of that one month during which I was active there, I believe that the position of the Bosniak part of the Presidency, as well as that of Stjepan Kljuic who represented the HDZ but espoused a pro-Bosniak policy and was less important at the time because by that time the HDZ core members for busy forming Herceg-Bosna, their position was that the matter in Bosnia would be resolved by a NATO intervention, and Izetbegovic spoke frequently at Presidency sessions that by the 15th of August at the latest NATO would intervene and that would have a decisive impact in the context of the resolution of the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And I think that this anticipation had a negative impact on Izetbegovic's readiness to agree to any compromise in his discussions with the other parties. The Presidency was more of a screen for the world in general, and this can be said of the government at the time as well because to all intents and purposes Izetbegovic pursued his policies basically through the leadership of the SDA. By way of illustration, officially the minister of the interior was Alija Delimustafic; however, Izetbegovic did these sort of affairs through Bakir Alispahic rather than through Delimustafic. He was the head of the town security service and he was a party loyal and through Hasan Cengic who didn't have any official positions at the time but he was in charge of military affairs within the party. So keep up the appearances of it all functioning in a multi-ethnic way, there were these bodies of the government and the Presidency, but as you went deeper down the real powers were wielded within towns and in Bosnia-Herzegovina -- well, I cannot say it was only the Bosniak and Muslim people, but people from the SDA who wielded power in these positions. I'm sorry if I can say this. Divjak was often times mentioned as a Serb who was in the military leadership and it's true that he was among the top three men in the BH army, but if you go further down the chain you won't find a single colonel or a lieutenant-colonel, et cetera, who would be occupying an even slightly significant position who wasn't a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And when was it that you realised the way the SDA worked and what was the view expressed by it -- by the elite which joined Zulfikarpasic when they broke away from them?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: A moment ago you revealed to us what the decision-making mechanisms were within the SDA and the government in general. Can you tell us how did the SDA take decisions and what sort of view was taken of this by the Bosniak elite that joined Zulfikarpasic and broke away from them?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, the circles that or the circle around Zulfikarpasic was a very narrow one. From the more prominent figures there was a professor of Faculty of Philosophy --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- who joined Zulfikarpasic. At the time I was in the Presidency, they were critical of Izetbegovic's policies. I had occasion to speak to Muhamed Filipovic, there was Pejanovic there. Even before Pejanovic and I joined the Presidency I -- we could hear Muhamed Filipovic speaking very critically of Izetbegovic and his views. We would even have discussions with Izetbegovic, and Filipovic, together with Pejanovic and myself, expressed serious criticism of the way the government was run in Sarajevo. As you may know, the authorities in Sarajevo and Bosnia-Herzegovina -- well, that was one and the same for us. When you said "authorities in Sarajevo," it meant the authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina because we did not have much contact with those outside of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Hasan Cengic and Alispahic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just for record, can you repeat the name of the professor from Faculty of Philosophy who joined Zulfikarpasic. Interpreters didn't catch it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The name is Muhamed Filipovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us -- you mentioned Hasan Cengic and then Alispahic. Can you tell us, what were the main personal factors in Alija Izetbegovic's circle and what was their political position?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Even then it was known and ever since the war the Bosniak papers in Sarajevo write about the SDA being led during the war by the convicts group that comprised other people around Alija Izetbegovic who had also been convicted of Muslim nationalism or pan-Islamism. Izetbegovic's Islamic Declaration was a sort of foundation or a programme, a platform, if you will, around which they had gathered and which was at the centre of that process. It was not only a religious or theological work, but also a political platform which would reflect upon Izetbegovic's subsequent behaviour in politics. Nowadays his son Bakir Izetbegovic, who is a member of the Presidency, in his statement immediately upon being elected to the Presidency, he stated that even today he was keeping the Islamic Declaration on his desk, by which he wanted to say that he still adhered to that text, programatic text. If you were referring to the people in the party leadership, apart from Cengic there was also Omer Behmen, Rusid Prguda, Edhem Bicakcic, Husein Zivalj, the aforementioned Hasan Cengic, and a few people more. But I must also add that these people or at least some of them never had transparent high positions in the public administration. They remained in the shadow. Hasan Cengic who was in charge of military matters and never was in a high position until after the war --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think we heard enough. Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I actually become a bit concerned. We know that the witness is under a considerable time constraint and I have also two hours of cross-examination and now we hear a lot of things, including the views of Bakir Izetbegovic, which are definitely not relevant in this case. So I think -- I'm getting worried that here that time is wasted, that I at the end will not have for the cross-examination. So I think there should be some limitations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. How much more do you have for your examination-in-chief, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one more question -- actually, one and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Professor Kecmanovic, was it your conclusion or impression or did you have information about the reliability --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the accused please repeat the question. The interpreter didn't understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. The interpreters were not able to understand you. Could you repeat your question, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I kindly ask that one question to be separated from the half question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: My first question is: Did you have information and did you reach a conclusion about the reliability in implementing what had been agreed between the Serb and the Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: In my statement I pointed out this characteristic of the late Alija Izetbegovic who was known for changing his opinion, and he was a good man to talk to at leisure, but he was an very unpleasant negotiator because he would often change positions. On one occasion he even said that he had one opinion in the morning and another in the afternoon, and that was criticised as inconsistency and unreliability. I cannot say that Izetbegovic had a tendency to slight his partners in talks, but maybe it was a feature of his character. There was an opinion that this was the result of pressure being exerted on Izetbegovic from within his party, various factions in his party. But some of his closest co-workers did say that he took most decisions himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And the Serbian side, what -- or rather, the SDS, how reliable were they?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: In this respect I think that the SDS and you personally were much more consistent and more direct, to my mind even a bit too much so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. You will probably get the opportunity to speak about the reasons of your -- of your separation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I have an intervention about the transcript. On page 33, line 18, "pan-Islamism" was omitted and "Islamic fundamentalism." Both should have been recorded, first pan-Islamism and later on Islamic fundamentalism because that's what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you confirm that, Mr. Kecmanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I confirm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. As you have noted, Mr. Kecmanovic, your evidence in chief in this case has been admitted in its most part in writing, that is, through your written statement. And now you'll be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor after a break of half an hour. We'll resume at quarter past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Kecmanovic.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Dr. Kecmanovic, at the outset of this cross-examination I would like to thank you for attending an interview with the Prosecution on Wednesday and I will come back to some of the facts that you told us during this interview as we go. And one other remark, as we discussed during this interview we have only very limited time for the cross-examination, and therefore I would kindly ask you to answer my question as short and focused as possible. This morning, Dr. Kecmanovic, you described what your party, the Alliance of Reform Forces of Yugoslavia for Bosnia-Herzegovina was standing for, and this policy of your party essentially put you into opposition to the nationalist parties which you referred to this morning as mono-ethnic parties, and that would include the SDS as well; right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you also described this morning that basically the SDA party was the power centre and not so much the official organs and you described Izetbegovic being in the power centre as such surrounded by his other people. The same would apply to the SDS, would it not? It was the power centre of the Bosnian Serbs; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Which period are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I'm referring to the period before the -- immediately before the war and before the official organs of Republika Srpska were established. So before the outbreak of the war.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I can say that it wasn't really the same thing. In the Serbian Democratic Party the distribution of power, as it were, in the party was greater. There were some people who were almost on the same footing with Karadzic and they were candidates for some positions. Likewise, Karadzic at the very beginning was not the first man of the party; that position was vacant. They had a sort of collective leadership. As is stated there, I was the one supposed to fill that position, but --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you. I was actually referring to the situation before -- immediately before the outbreak of the war, and when you were actually having discussions with Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Karadzic, at that point in time Mr. Karadzic was definitely the power centre in the SDS party and the SDS party was actually the body that counted at that point in time, was it not?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: You mean the time before the leadership of the SDA left this city and went to Pale --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: SDS.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me explain so we understand each other better. We must distinguish the period until -- including the co-operation of the three ethnic parties and the period when the SDS withdrew from the joint bodies and left, which period are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Actually, I thought I was quite precise. I was talking about the period when you had the talks - you and Mr. Pejanovic - had the talks with Krajisnik and Karadzic. That was the period and that was the talk I was referring to.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: All right. So it's the period when they had already left the common bodies in Sarajevo, I mean the Serbian representatives. Obviously there were several people on an equal footing, but Karadzic was number 1 nominally. I communicated with Krajisnik, Koljevic, Karadzic, and that shows that the leadership was more of a collective thing, certainly more so than on the Muslim side. Karadzic was the number one man in reality and also formally, but you could also speak about a collective leadership.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, I take it that you can scroll back the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: At page 37, line 14, was your question about SDA party or SDS party?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Line 14.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No, I actually -- I spoke about the SDS party -- SDA party being the power centre. That's what he told us this morning and I was referring to the SDS being --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ah, yes, I missed it. Yes. Thank you. The same would apply to the --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would also like to intervene in the transcript at this juncture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 38, line 1, Dr. Kecmanovic said -- apart from saying that there were a number of people who were on the same footing with Karadzic and who were candidates, but it was not recorded that Karadzic did not run.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably -- do you confirm, Mr. Kecmanovic, what Mr. Karadzic indicated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's continue, please Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Dr. Kecmanovic, in paragraph 5 of your statement you refer to the criticism that you received after joining the BiH Presidency. You are aware that the term "Izetbegovic" or "Alija's own private Serbs" was used by Mr. Karadzic when referring to you and that participate -- and your participation in the work of the BiH institutions; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know -- or actually, I don't know that it was Karadzic personally who said that, but I know that people from the RS leadership spoke about that. You also had the opposite case, the Muslim side spoke about Karadzic's Serbs --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Sir, I'm not asking about opposite cases. I just asked you to be precise and answer just the question I asked and not tell a story from the other side.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: So can we please have 65 ter 15 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see, if I may just for a moment. I do want us to work efficiently in this cross-examination, but sometimes such digressions are in the function of an explanation what that really means. It was customary for all three sides for people who were not included in the ethnic movement to consider them traitors or Radovan's people or something. It was, as I said, usual at the time and was not seen as an insult.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we please have 15896 on the screen, 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And as it is coming up, it is an announcement by Mr. Karadzic dated the 2nd of June, 1992, in which he refers to you and Mr. Pejanovic joining the Presidency as somewhat illegal. If you look at the box in your language it's this box you find there. He mentioned that somewhat illegal and refers to you as private Serbs of Alija Izetbegovic. And he, in fact, even compares you with the private Serbs of Ante Pavelic. Dr. Kecmanovic, he compares you here with the Serbs co-operating with the Croat leader Pavelic, an ally of the Nazi Germany during the Second World War; right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't know about what you have just showed me, and this really is a serious insult but this is the first time I see this.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And the publication "Nas Glas" is what? Is it a daily or ... ?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. This is news to me. I've never seen this before.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript please. May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Firstly, on page 40 it was not recorded what Dr. Kecmanovic said, that the Muslim side called some Serbs Karadzic's Serbs and the Serbian side Alija's Serbs. And I kindly ask the witness to be allowed to read this whole article to really see if he was compared to Ante Pavelic as has been suggested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If necessary, you may take up the issue later on, but I think the witness had opportunity to read this and the question was fair enough. Shall we continue, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. Can this exhibit be -- please be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour, the witness has said that: "I don't know. This is news to me. I've never seen this before." So I don't think there's any foundation to admit it through this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it not related to his statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, it's not related to his credibility, so, and it's a question of foundation, actually, as opposed to relevance.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was discussing with the witness basically that he was -- that he was called Alija's Serbs and those kind of things and he confirmed this. And now I showed -- and he said that he didn't know that Karadzic said that. And I showed him an example. And the fact that he just didn't see that before doesn't mean that he has not now referred to it and dealt with it, so I think there is a foundation laid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6350, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Dr. Kecmanovic, in paragraph 5 of your statement you also say that such things would be said publicly for propaganda purposes and were not really meant. Is it your evidence that Dr. Karadzic had in these cases when he would say such things, would he mislead the public? Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that this was in the function of propaganda. I can't believe that he meant that sincerely. Even if he had meant that, he would not have advocated for me to lead the SDS. He personally advocated that. Therefore, he could not sincerely think what he said and what he wrote. Otherwise, he would not have spoken to me later on on several occasions. At the end of the day, he invited me to this Tribunal as a Defence witness; otherwise, perhaps the Prosecution would have called me as a Prosecution witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Dr. Kecmanovic, the purpose of such what you call propaganda would be to cause outrage against dissidents from the nationalist agenda that the SDS pursued; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: You see, all the three nationalist parties including the SDS participated in the elections, and one such convincing majorities in the elections that they didn't feel any special need to gather around themselves a relatively small - to my great disappointment - a relatively small number of people who voted for some other parties, including my mine.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And the purpose of such propaganda, calling someone Alija's Serbs comparable to Ante Pavelic's Serbs, that purpose would also be to put pressure on you and others to not express any views outside the ethnocentric policy of the Bosnian Serb leadership and not work in the Bosnian institution; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: You see, when it comes to the people who may have participated in the institutions on one or the other side, we're not talking about people at large. We're talking about individuals who do -- do not cave in under such pressures. They behave autonomously. I could have joined the SDS at any moment. I would have been admitted with open arms before the elections and after the elections, but even that did not sway me to change my mind and become a member of the SDS. I believe that this applies in general terms to people of my kind who were subjected to the same kind of pressure and propaganda, as you call it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Dr. Kecmanovic, you resigned from the BiH Presidency in July 1992, and before you did that there was considerable pressure on you from the Bosnian Serb leadership to do that; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Pressure not to become a member of the Presidency? Is that what you're asking me?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No, I was asking you -- I was referring to the fact that you resigned in July 1992, and I asked you whether it's right -- correct that before you did it you got pressure from the Bosnian Serb leadership to do so?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I was under no pressure. Nobody put any pressure on me. All that was my autonomous decision. If I had caved in to such pressures, I would have probably been the leader of the SDS or I would have joined it later on or something of that kind. There was no pressure put to bear on me.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Dr. Kecmanovic, there is evidence before this Trial Chamber --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I refer here to the 14th Republika Srpska Presidency Session of the 3rd of July, 1992, and it's D438 under point 2 and point 12.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: -- and I'm just referring to this here, Mr. -- Dr. Kecmanovic. They say here in this record that you, Mr. Pejanovic, Mr. Simovic, Mr. Nikolic, and other Serbs shall be publicly invited to withdraw from their positions in the official bodies in the -- in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And you are aware of such public invitations, are you not?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I almost don't know about those invitations. The situation in Sarajevo was such that I didn't have the time to follow such matters, especially when I started working in the Presidency. It -- I was familiar with that to a certain extent. Somebody conveyed that to me, perhaps Simovic or Pejanovic. But I really did not pay much attention to that. I perceived that as an expected reaction.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Equally, this Trial Chamber has evidence in front of it --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I refer now to D440, that's the 15th RS Presidency Session of 6 July.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: -- and there a position was adopted on talks that Messrs. Koljevic and Krajisnik should have with you and Mr. Pejanovic. It states under item 3 in this session that they were appointed to conduct such talks and that the aim of the talks would be to determine conditions for your resignation. They even formulated demands you should put to Mr. Izetbegovic. Dr. Kecmanovic, these talks did take place, did they not?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: The Defence team showed me this document, therefore I'm familiar with it. I had not seen it before that. I can give you a very precise answer to your question. Perhaps the accused Karadzic can help me with that. I don't doubt that such a decision was adopted. This is, after all, an official document. However, when I was in Pale before proceeding towards Belgrade, not for a single moment did any such matter came up, no such talks were conducted. I did not sit down with Krajisnik and Koljevic in any official capacity and nothing of that kind was told me. The late Professor Koljevic waited for me in Lukavica. We went to Pale together. We were met by Karadzic, Plavsic, and Krajisnik there. First we had dinner and we talked over dinner. Then we had some one-on-one talks on the following day and on the day after. Nobody gave me any conditions to comply with. The talks never went in that direction at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let's move on to another topic. In your statement you several times refer to the fact that the policies of the SDS and your own party were similar. Dr. Kecmanovic, that refers basically to the fact that both parties at some point in time wanted that Bosnia-Herzegovina remain part of Yugoslavia; right? That was where you basically agreed; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And when the former Yugoslavia was no longer an option in April 1992, the Bosnian Serb leadership wanted to have a state of their own in certain territories in Bosnia-Herzegovina; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't put it that way. I believe that it was more about creating a confederal or federal union, some sort of a union or a structure that would be based on the territorial and ethnic concentrations of the population. As far as my party is concerned, after the changes that you have just mentioned, there were some shifts in the positions. In my party we supported that concept that was also a concept advocated by the Cutileiro's commission of the European Union. A new situation had arisen, so it was decided that there would be cantons. Entities were not mentioned, but rather cantons or semi-cantons. The Swiss model came up quite often, the Belgian model. In any case we sought for more realistic solutions.
