More or less, everybody participated in that. I believe the SDP was the only party that kept on insisting on a centralised and unitarian structure of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In my party manifesto, the territorial and ethnic issue was not a priority. We spoke about the division that would be based on historical demographic, geographical traffic conditions, and finally on territorial and ethnic principle, and this is that would end up in the platform of the Presidency --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you. I didn't want to hear so many details of the period before when there was still the Cutileiro Plan. I was actually referring to the fact that after April 1992 when Yugoslavia in the former was not existing anymore, that was the period I was asking for and you did not answer that question. Dr. Kecmanovic, in paragraph 54 of --

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Please, let's clarify things. I want to answer rather than skip a question of yours.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But I had asked you a concrete question. I spoke about the period after April 1992, and then I said the Bosnian Serb leadership wanted a state of their own. And then you spoke about something completely different.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Then my short answer would be: As far as I know, they didn't want a state of their own. They wanted Bosnia-Herzegovina to be transformed into a union, federation, or confederation of territorial and ethnic units of all the three peoples. Is that okay for an answer?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let's move on. Dr. Kecmanovic, in paragraph 54 of your statement you refer to an expert report which you prepared for Prijedor. And in the interview on Wednesday you also spoke about this expert report and you -- that you prepared it for the Kvocka case --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is case number IT-98-30/1.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And I'm just -- want to refer you to a passage that is in there and as you remember this report and you remembered it well during the interview, I see no reason that we have to pull it up in e-court. In your Kvocka report --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And that is 65 ter 25087 for the Defence to know.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: -- you have a section: The Muslim-Croatian war. You probably remember this, Dr. Kecmanovic, that you have this report and this section or do we have to pull it up?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: That was a report. It was not a testimony; right?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No, it was a report. It was a report that you prepared in the Kvocka case and you had a section in there where you described the Muslim-Croatian war. And in that section --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And for the Defence to know, it's on page 34 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: -- you say -- or better, wrote: "Essentially" --

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I would love to see it in an electronic form, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Okay. Good. We can do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we please have 65 ter 25087 and we need the page 34 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And in the B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: There is, unfortunately, Your Honour, there is no B/C/S --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We have only six pages.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No. You should have actually the entire report. There is a B/C/S only of six pages and that's the Prijedor part, but I'm referring to the main part of the report and that is -- the English version e-court page 34.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So shall we show from page 31, then, which has the title, the Muslim-Croatian war.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Can we have --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you kindly provide me with a translation, if not in e-court perhaps a hard copy could be provided, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We do not have a hard copy either --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll print out from page 31 to page 34 and we'll provide it to you in a moment. Yes, please in the meantime --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. I'm just -- can we move to the page 34 in e-court. And it's only a small -- yes. And it's actually at the very top.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It says here on the very top: "Essentially, it was an inevitable war that arose from the very logic of the Muslim and Croatian movements, which, just like the Serbian, aspired to create their own ethnic space and establish their own nation states." Mr. -- Dr. Kecmanovic, you are saying here that the Muslims and the Croats and the Serbians aspired to create their own ethnic space and establish their own nation states. That's what you wrote in your report that was tendered in a case before this Tribunal. Are you now saying that's wrong?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Shall we wait until the witness receives the hard copy.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have not received the translation that I asked for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's on top of page 32. We don't have it in your language, unfortunately. Page 32 in hard copy, but page 34 in e-court. Probably you heard the translation of that sentence. Yes, can you answer the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can. I would like to have the text before me. It would make things easier, but I can answer anyway. Could you please repeat your question, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I have asked you before -- I asked you whether the SDS or the Serbian -- Bosnian Serb people wanted to create their own state. You said no they didn't. And then I quoted to you what I quoted to you, and then I asked you -- but you are saying it here, right here.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, you see, I'm talking about here not only about Serbs but also Croats and Muslims. And that statement seems to be contradictory to what I stated in the report on the face of it. However, we're talking about somewhat broader considerations of the problem. Just a while ago I mentioned the term "confederation of unions." In any case, those would have been areas where -- which in either the confederal option or a unionist option would give security to all of the three peoples who had -- who had very negative historical experiences, and those experiences accumulated from one generation to the next. There was the 1941, 1918, and other historical events that had created uncertainties and concerns that had accumulated through generations. There was hostilities, needs to take revenge, and certain things. And they may have been suppressed either by the goodwill of the people or under the oppression of the communist regime. However, deep down it existed, and in the moments of crisis such sentiments surfaced to the ground. And it seemed that all the three peoples wanted something of that sort.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Dr. Kecmanovic, you speak here in this sentence of inevitable war, and in this context I would like to address paragraph 56 in your statement where you express your belief that it was possible to transform Bosnia-Herzegovina territorially and ethnically without any radical or forced changes to the ethnic structure on the ground. You also say here in that paragraph that the metaphor about the leopard and his spots which apparently faithfully reflects the highly mixed ethnic composition of Bosnia is largely a construct. Dr. Kecmanovic, you yourself used this very same metaphor in your expert report that we are looking at here at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And can we please have page 21 in the e-court, page 21. Is that page 21? No. Can we have page 21. 21 of the report that we just spoke about. It's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: E-court page.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We speak about 65 ter 25087, e-court page 21.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, collapse the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Kecmanovic, given that we do not have the translation, providing the English version in hard copy seems to be of no point. If you could take a look at the monitor, we zoomed in sufficiently or hear the translation which will be read -- relayed to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We are looking at the chapter 3, "National Visions of the Break-up of Bosnia-Herzegovina." And if we zoom in on the second paragraph under this chapter, it says: "A fall-back position for all three peoples was that if none of them could take the entire republic in the direction they desired, they could divide it on the basis of their right to national self-determination including secession. The problem, however, lay in the fact that the territorial and ethnic structure of Bosnia-Herzegovina resembled a leopard's skin. Large concentrations of a given group outside the larger multi-ethnic towns were not mutually connected. Party headquarters on all three sides were feverishly preoccupied with ethnic maps." And in the next paragraph it says: "But in vain, because none of them could combine unconnected, ethnically homogeneous enclaves into nationally compact cantons and at the same time avoid massive movements of people, both their own and those of the two other ethnic groups. Neither Muslims, Serbs, nor Croats were prepared to either leave their homes or stay in them as national minority. As in an ancient tragedy, each side consistently followed the line of its national interests, which could have been accepted if viewed separately, but which, when they intersected, led inevitably to the catastrophic outcome of civil war." And, Dr. Kecmanovic, that is what you wrote in the Kvocka report and was what unfolded after the outbreak of the conflict was, indeed, massive ethnic cleansing, was it not?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: What was massive ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What unfolded in Bosnia-Herzegovina; for instance, in Banja Luka; for instance, in Foca; for instance, in Eastern Bosnia; and around Sarajevo, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Not around but in Sarajevo. Do you agree? I mean, Sarajevo is the most traumatic example of it because the highest number of inhabitants left Sarajevo. If you compare it to the other figures of inhabitants leaving their native areas, the highest number of departures was in Sarajevo. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We'll come to did your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Do you agree then, Mr. Kecmanovic, that in Banja Luka, Foca, and in Eastern Bosnia ethnic cleansing took place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would not call it ethnic cleansing because it has a different connotation at least in the circumstances of Bosnia-Herzegovina because this is a reference to ethnic cleansing on one side only, whereas ethnic cleansing took place on all three sides.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But you would view as ethnic cleansing what happened inside the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would simply call all these events with a single term rather than referring to certain events in one part of the country as ethnic cleansing and to other events in other parts of countries as simply resettlement of peoples.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I object to the misrepresentation of what Mr. Kecmanovic said in his report. He spoke of massive movements rather than ethnic cleansing. Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff translated "massive movements" into "ethnic cleansings."

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is an intervention that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Inappropriate. Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, can the two pages be admitted, it's page 19 -- e-court page 21 and e-court page 34.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would, however, kindly ask to be provided with this section of the report in B/C/S in the course of my testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Unfortunately, we don't have it at the moment. Probably it might -- somewhere it exists at the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I actually have discussed it also with you, Dr. Kecmanovic, and asked you whether you have the B/C/S version and it was my understanding that you do have the B/C/S version of this report. What we do have -- we looked everywhere. We only had the translation of these six pages related to Prijedor but Mr. Iain could not find any B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's where we are, Mr. Kecmanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the situation is such that we simply cannot discuss the matter without the necessary material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have any objection, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll admit those two pages as well as the first page of the document, cover page.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6351, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would like now to move on to the platform, the platform that you worked on in the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina and you mentioned this platform in paragraph 11 of your statement and I think you mentioned it also today.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And can we please have 65 ter 25060 in e-court. And we have here both languages again.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And we can see from the second page, from the second page but maybe we do not have to look at it now, from the second page we can see it was adopted on the 26th of June, 1992. When we -- can we look at point 4. If we look at point 4, that's this -- the second page in both languages, we see conditions -- we see conditions for peace negotiations listed, and among them are: (a), the secession of hostilities; (b), the establishment of the political situation before the aggression; (d) compensation; (c) -- but I read (d), compensation for the war damages and punishment of the perpetrators. And at the end of this paragraph it says: "Bosnia and Herzegovina will not accept negotiations which have as their basis the establishment of ethnically pure territories or a regional division of Bosnia and Herzegovina on a solely ethnic basis. Bosnia and Herzegovina will never accept any kind of territorial or demographic changes and advantages which have resulted from war and violence." Dr. Kecmanovic, that is what you together with your colleagues in the Presidency made their goals; right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Let me add that certain amendments were made in addition to what the conclusions were not only of the working group but also of the Presidency. For instance, in the preamble to this paper, mention is made of the aggression on the part of Yugoslavia or the JNA against Bosnia-Herzegovina. This was not in our version and it was added at a later date by --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the name of the person.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- at the Presidency, but let's go back to what you're interested in.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. This -- I actually asked you that this is what you and your colleagues have agreed about and you actually drafted it. So --

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. You see, a moment ago I did say that the basis for the platform was a document adopted by my party, in fact. I made sure that it was used and I did say that earlier on after insisting that Bosnia-Herzegovina stay within Yugoslavia we accepted Cutileiro's proposal and the conference on Bosnia-Herzegovina as the basis and that's -- please allow me to finish. You say --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No, no, wait a minute. We have very little time, and therefore --

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: -- as you -- I understand that you want to tell the whole story, but we do not have time for the whole story and so we have to, unfortunately, restrict ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can this please be admitted, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, a direct answer to your question. It reads here not on the -- not on a solely ethnic basis. So ethnicity was not taken as a sole criterion but as one of. Do you see this?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: There is another place where you quoted something where this issue is also being relativised. I don't know if you agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I actually have read it this way. In English it is the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6352, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Line 23, page 56, it turned out that this was -- what was said was that this was added at a later stage by Ganic and Ganic was not recorded in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did the -- when you met the Bosnian Serb leadership in Pale, you conveyed these platform goals, did you not?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: No. You see, this was a public document and I think that they were aware of this without my playing a part in it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And when you'd had your talks in Pale, the Bosnian Serb leadership did not agree to these goals and conditions for negotiations; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we simply didn't discuss it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we please have Exhibit 65 ter 25069A on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And as it is coming up, and you will see it in a minute, it's an excerpt from the Bosnia-Herzegovina 128th Presidency Session of the 24th of June, where you indeed discuss the platform. And it's only an excerpt because it is a lengthy record, but as you mentioned in the interview that we had you are aware of the Presidency sessions and you indeed reviewed them in anticipation of your testimony. Can we please have page 3 in the English and page 4 in the B/C/S. And we have here Mr. Akmadzic. In the lower part, he says: "Those prerequisites are: 'Cease war operations, recognition of the single system of government, and negotiations which have as their foundation the creation of pure ethnic territories cannot be accepted.'" That's basically what we also saw in the document. And you all agreed in the Presidency about this; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: May I have the entire document?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We are not going into details of the entire document and we are only discussing this page here, and what I just mentioned was how Mr. Akmadzic summarises it and at the very bottom he says the following. He refers to the extreme militant faction within the SDS and that the Presidency had opted not to speak to them. To whom is Mr. Akmadzic referring when he speaks about the extreme militant faction within the SDS, can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Truly, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we please have the next page in both languages, and we are again looking at the lower part.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And, in fact, you yourself are speaking here and you make clear that the starting point is the situation as it was before the war and that any kind of changes within the national structure of the populations that were created by war, moving away, et cetera, will not be accepted.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And can we please have page 6 in both languages, and in the B/C/S we look at the last sentence and in the English we look at the upper part.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And in fact you say here, Dr. Kecmanovic, those are territorial ethnic changes caused by violence, war, genocide, moving away, et cetera. That refers to what we just some minutes ago spoke about, that is, the expulsion of population, crimes, and you even refer to genocide, that activities had taken place, and you wanted this to be reversed; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Of course this is an accurate reflection of what was said. Of course I was not in favour of acknowledging anything that is the result of violence, genocide, of course, or migrations. At any rate, it did happen. And of course it is very difficult to establish what is the result of violence and what the various departures were motivated by. I can give you examples of persons who did not suffer any violence and yet did move to other areas where members of their ethnicity were present simply because they felt safer and better there.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But during the Presidency sessions, you received information about such violent acts; correct? Mr. Halilovic reported about it. You heard others. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: See, I did hear it from Halilovic, whose report I did not trust that much. I trusted my own eyes and what I observed in Sarajevo, and that was violence that was suffered by the Serbian people.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can this please be admitted, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask one thing? Is the Serbian side identical to the English? I'm interested in the first line where Kecmanovic says that it is inappropriate to name the person by their first and last names, the persons that you do not want to speak to. And I don't see this in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It's a different page. It's a different page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can that page be received as well, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Given that it is only a seven-page document, we'll admit it in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. I would -- actually, what I have done is I selected the sections where there is a discussion ongoing on a certain topic. I never just had one page. I always had a certain section.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Exhibit P6353.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Dr. Kecmanovic, in your statement in paragraph 35 you speak about your impression that the leadership in Pale was very concerned about what was happening in Sarajevo and that for them what was happening in the other parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina was of secondary importance.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we please have 65 ter 25085 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And, Dr. Kecmanovic, as it is coming up it is again just a -- no, I think we have both languages. We should actually have both. No, that can't be it. I have this actually it looks different in what I have, "Seasons in Hell."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Check the 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No, the 65 ter number is correct, but we have it actually in a different format so that two pages are all on -- oh, I see we have it in this format, but of course it's a bit difficult to read. The B/C/S -- let's then see.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What we have here indeed is an excerpt from Mr. Ed Vulliamy's book "Seasons in Hell." Mr. -- Dr. Kecmanovic, you know Mr. Vulliamy, the journalist; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: He -- and if we look at page 1, last paragraph -- can we see the -- can we see the other page, this -- yes, this side? Can we look at -- no, the previous again, the previous. In the last paragraph -- yes, the last paragraph. Now I have it. In the last paragraph Mr. Vulliamy describes a conversation he had with Nikola Koljevic in Belgrade, during which Koljevic admitted to the journalist that Sarajevo was designated the piece of violent theatre which would captivate the world's attention and draw it away from the principal programme. And if we now move to -- again to the other side, yes. And he says: "It amazes me that you all took so long to get to the point. Poor Sarajevo! That was all you could think about. The crossroads of Europe! None of you had ever been on holiday in Trnopolje ..." Do you know about this meeting in summer 1992 between Koljevic/Vulliamy and did you perhaps attend?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Then we move on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Dr. Kecmanovic, during the interview we heard you said that you were not aware of the six strategic goals of the Bosnian Serbs, and, sir, there's evidence before this Court that the first strategic goal of the Bosnian Serb leadership was the separation of the Serbian people from the other two national communities. And further on, Dr. Kecmanovic, we have evidence before this Trial Chamber that this strategic goal means, as Mr. Karadzic explains in the 16th Session of the Assembly of the Serbian people of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that is on the 12th of May, 1992 --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, that's 65 ter, or rather, P956, e-court page 9.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: -- and he says: "It means separation from those who are our enemies and who have used every opportunity, especially in this century, to attack us and who would continue with such practices if we were to continue to stay together in the same state." Dr. Kecmanovic, you said you were not aware of this session and what Karadzic said there, but given your interest in participation and participation in politics at that time, you must have been aware that Mr. Karadzic and the Bosnian Serb leadership saw the Croats and the Muslims as the enemy of the Serbs. You were -- you knew that; right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Not a priori as enemies. That would have been inconceivable, to consider a whole people as hostile. I never heard Karadzic say that or heard that being said about him. The political leaderships and leaderships of ethnic parties would discuss these issues and there would be confrontations in that sense only.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, we'll stop here and we'll have a break if it is convenient.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll have a break for 45 minutes and resume at quarter past 1.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.29 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we continue, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff. Mr. Robinson, the Chamber will grant your reply -- your request for reply to the Prosecution's response regarding videolink testimony of Nikola Poplasen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, we'll be able to file that today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Dr. Kecmanovic, you were aware that the Bosnian Serb leadership did not want to live together with the Muslims any longer; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: You see, that must all be viewed in the context of the fact that the Muslims, together with the Croats, actually made that co-existence impossible because they imposed relations of unequality on us after out-voting the Serbian representatives in the Assembly and the government and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: So the answer was yes?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I think it wasn't merely the opinion of the leadership of the RS but also that of the Serbian people since it was put into the position of being dominated by the other two peoples, that was reactive. It was imposed upon them.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In this regard I just want to quote to you something from the 17th Session of the Republika Srpska Assembly dated 24th and 26th July 1992. That's D92, page 86. And Mr. Karadzic is speaking about the Muslims and to be with them -- the impossibility to be with them in a unitary state. And I quote: "We know very well the fundamentalism -- what the fundamentalism is and that we can't live together. There is no tolerance. They quadruple through birth-rate and we Serbs are not up to that. Not only are the Serbs not up to that, but the Christians in Lebanon are not up to that Oriental mentality stemming from Islam." These kind of arguments made publicly, you are aware of this, the birth-rate and all these kind of things; right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with this specific statement by Karadzic that you have quoted, but the example of Lebanon is very telling because that's where a prosperous country fell apart, it was called the Switzerland of the Arab world, because the demographic changes that were in favour of the Muslims was such that the Muslim population demanded more power because of their growing share in the structure of the overall population.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we please have 65 ter 25024 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And as it is coming up, it is an article that you, Dr. Kecmanovic, wrote in Nin, a Belgrade daily, on the 20th of January, 1995, with the title: "Lava Cooling."

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Again, can we please have page 2 in the English and we look at the last, the very last, paragraph, and then we move on to the next page as I'm reading. And in the -- in the B/C/S it's page 1, also the last paragraph. And then while I'm reading we go over to the page 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What you are saying here, and I quote, you speak about Izetbegovic first and then you say: "At the same time, on the other side, in addition to territorial and ethnic separation from the Muslims ... Pale demand in the form of an ultimatum to also be connected with Serbia as its national mother country. However, on this side of the Drina River, after the dissolution of the SFRY, there remains tens of thousands of Sandzak Muslims living there without any demarcation. Moreover, having fled across the river, numerous Bosnian and Herzegovinian Muslims joined them as refugees. "When they meet their countrymen Serbs from Bosnia here in Belgrade, they ask each other why could they not live together on equal terms back home, since they can do ... here as refugees." When it says here, Dr. Kecmanovic, "Pale demand," that would be Mr. Karadzic and the Bosnian Serb leadership; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Clearly you are merely -- you have merely read a fragment. But we must read the text as a whole. It was ironically written and in a humorous tone although the topic is serious. The Serbs considered the Muslims to have been Christians originally who embraced Islam, whereas the Bosniaks consider the Serbs to be original Muslims who converted to Christianity. In the subheading of the text we can see that it is untenable that people of different ethnic or political affiliations must live together. After all, today in all parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina there are members of all three ethnicities as minorities, and in Banja Luka there are significant numbers of Muslims and Croats whom I know and I socialise with them as -- just as there are many Serbs who remained in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But I had actually asked you to deal with this particular paragraph, but in any event you call this the Bosnian paradox and that's a result -- this Bosnian paradox that you here describe is a result of ethnocentric policy of the Bosnian Serb leadership and their claim that there is no life together with the Muslims, is it not?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: No. In the whole 65 ter I relativise the question if living together is possible or living separately, and I conclude that these are relative things and that both options are possible. I also point out that the choice for ethnically homogeneous wholes, these choices were made by all three sides. And finally there are young people in all three communities, and I also have Bosniak friends in Sarajevo just as I know a number of Bosniaks who were close friends of Dr. Karadzic's.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let me --

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: And -- just a moment. What you have mentioned, Pale, you insist on this, Pale in this the text is a metaphor for a centre of the Serbian nation, Sarajevo as a metaphor for the Muslims. West Mostar or Grude a metaphor for the Croats. So that's the way to understand it without anybody specific at Pale in mind. That was the position of the entire people, not only of their leadership --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you --

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: -- just a moment --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No, no, let me interrupt you here --

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: -- may I interrupt you --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: -- I interrupt you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Kecmanovic, I think you answered the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And I only wanted to --

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: If I may --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We have no time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Kecmanovic, if necessary, Mr. Karadzic will take up the issue in his re-examination, rest assured. The Chamber will monitor that you will be able to speak whatever you wish to and have to.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript, please. In line 23 it was not recorded what Mr. Kecmanovic said, namely, that he personally knew Karadzic's Muslim friends. That was not recorded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In this -- the next -- the very next paragraph in this article you write the following: "'For us Serbs, there is no life together with the Muslims!' That is one of the most frequently used programme slogans of the Serbian national movement in Bosnia ..." And, Dr. Kecmanovic, on top of this movement stood the Bosnian Serb leadership; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I kindly ask the President of the Trial Chamber to caution the Prosecutor not to interrupt me and constantly mentioning the shortage of time. I'm not short of time. I have time -- I have hours and hours. I can stay as much as you want. The organisational problems that there may exist are no problems of mine. And now if you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Kecmanovic, we'll make sure that you have the opportunity to answer the question to the extent necessary and relevant. The Chamber will ensure that you speak out when it is relevant and necessary. At the previous time, because I find that you answered already sufficiently, we agreed with Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff. But -- yes, shall we continue?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just wanted to make now an observation.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: That we are hurrying so much through what we wanted to discuss is basically due to the fact that you have indicated through the Victims and Witnesses Unit and the Defence that you cannot continue to stay here. If that of course would change, we would have more time and we could be much more detailed. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that is the case. I confirm.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You know, I've been here since Sunday, which means five or six full days at the disposal of the team and this Tribunal and I'm willing to return, but I can't stay longer at a time than I have already stayed now because of my commitments in Belgrade and Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we continue?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Can this document be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, but I don't think we heard the answer from your last question.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: So I had asked you that: Mr. Karadzic was on top of the Serbian national movement, was he not? That was my question.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: He was at the head of the national movement because the Serbian people elected him to that position. In other words, he reflected the mood and the opinion of his voters.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can this document please be admitted, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6354, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: During the interview we had on Wednesday, you mentioned that given your professional background you are aware of the effect that propaganda has on various audiences; right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We spoke about that and your opinion was that propaganda had a decisive influence, to which I said that it was not the case, that it did have influence but not a decisive one otherwise we would have been able to resolve everything through propaganda, which means this would have been an attack on the principles of democracy, among which there is the position that people are of age and that they use their head to think.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In paragraph 43 and 49 of your statement in which you refer to the one-sided reporting and propaganda by the Bosnian BiH media portraying the Muslims as victims and the Serb soldiers as the sole perpetrators, that was the same just reversed for the Serbian propaganda; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and the Croatian too. When a civil war begins, naturally the media to a great extent are turned into propaganda tools. That's how it has always been everywhere. But the problem in this case, and I think I state that somewhere, that the so-called international propaganda almost fully sided with the Muslim side, which confused people about what it's all about. I even spoke about that to some of my Bosniak friends who were neutral with regard to both sides. They started to view the Serb side negatively because in our conversations when I was asking them what was happening, why they had changed their minds, they would reply, "But, you see that the whole world is supporting the Muslim side." They even mentioned the Russian side then that was at the time of Yeltsin and Kozyrev.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you. You are going into too many broad details. You confirmed when we talked that propaganda can cause fear; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And it can cause hatred; right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now we are really going into details, and given that you're in a hurry, this -- and this is a very fruitful topic, we could go on for a very long time. But yes, it does have a significant influence.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Dr. Kecmanovic, do you recall that when the rallies were taking place in 1990 and 1991 and in the parliaments, reference were made to the suffering of the Serbs during World War II. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I do not, but I know that in talks, even outside of institutions given the inter-ethnic tensions, among Serbs there was a lot of conjuring up of the Second World War when there was Pavelic's state and there was -- there were the same alliances against the Serbs now. And that 1991 the Muslims and Serbs -- the Muslims and Croats --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- joined forces against the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Dr. Kecmanovic, such kind of references was an important propaganda tool, was it not, because it was meant to remind the Serb audiences of the suffering of the nation and to cause this suffering, namely, the Croats and the Muslims; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think that any propaganda was required for that. I lived in Sarajevo since birth. No one of my friends and neighbours had such experiences in the previous generation. I can remind you of Pavelic's Budak's motto that one-third of the Serbs should be converted Catholicism, one-third expelled from Bosnia-Herzegovina, and one-third killed. That was part of Pavelic's ideology in the NDH. Children had to learn that at elementary school. It was part of the educational curriculum. We all knew that, although we were not there during the Second World War. But we all had a relative who came to harm in the Second World War. We didn't need Karadzic or the SDS to remind us.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. In paragraph 13 of your statement you describe that the Bosnian Presidency was constantly in session and in paragraph 28 you refer to the minutes of the Presidency. When you were not present during sessions you would get the minutes and transcript; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: No. This is an opportunity to point out a fact that has to do with the reliability of these minutes. When it was noted that I was absent from the sessions of the Presidency, even in October although in mid-August I resigned and sent it by fax to the Presidency and also informed the "Tanjug" which was published all over the region, but for September and October it is constantly stated that I wasn't present at Presidency sessions, as if I was still a member of the Presidency --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you --

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: -- this casts a shadow on --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: -- my question was actually answered. There was no need to digress. While you participated in Presidency session, you did discuss the expulsion of Muslims, did you not?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let me first go to 65 ter 25083, and it is the 124th Presidency Session, Bosnian Presidency Session, of 20 June 1992. And we would need the second page in the English and in the B/C/S. Mr. Kecmanovic, I'm aware that you were not present during this particular session, that is the one where the declaration of war was adopted. But I still would like to address one point and that is -- let's look at page 3 in the English and page 4 in the B/C/S and the last paragraph. Page 3 in the B/C/S -- in the English and 4 in the B/C/S. That's not correct. Page 3 in the English should be -- oh, yeah, I'm sorry, I'm sorry. If you look here it says in the last paragraph, there is a reference to: "The problem of the relocation of Muslims from Banja Luka, underlining that they received threats that they would be killed if they did not leave ..." And Mr. Izetbegovic said that if that would be tolerated, it would create ethnically pure regions and that the country should not succumb to this kind of pressure to establish ethnically pure regions. Dr. Kecmanovic, although you were not present, but this problem with Banja Luka and the expulsion of Muslims from there, that was a topic that you were aware of and you got information about; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: About these -- Izetbegovic's words, I didn't know anything about them nor did I attend the session. However, it is indicative that Izetbegovic was very concerned about the situation in Banja Luka, and the fact was that people were fleeing Sarajevo and they were even prevented from leaving Sarajevo. And that was never a topic at any of the sessions of the Presidency, although I wanted it to be discussed. Unlike Banja Luka, Sarajevo had an inner circle. It was encircled from the inside and the authorities in Sarajevo did not allow the people to leave the city. As far as I know about Banja Luka, I can't be a hundred per cent sure. People didn't have any problem in Banja Luka to leave it. As far as I know, I can't testify about something that I did not see with my own two eyes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This page?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The Presidency session.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: We don't object to the whole thing being admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's only three pages.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, it's only three pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6355, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Now I would like to have 65 ter 25071A on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And it is an excerpt of the Presidency session of 30 June 1992, and you were actually present on that occasion. And as it is coming up, you received information during Presidency sessions about the detention of non-Serb civilians; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: About detention of ... ?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Detention of non-Serb civilians in facilities run by Bosnian Serb forces, did you not?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Not in any detail. You mean in the territory outside of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I did not have any such specific information. As far as I can remember, we did not receive such information. If we received information, it was rather general. As a rule, it was not written. Sefer Halilovic as the Chief of the General Staff of the Bosniak army, which was known as the BiH army, during the session or the beginning of every session he would provide a very general report on the situation on the ground. He mostly referred to the victories of the Muslim side, i.e., the BiH army. The tone was very optimistic when he spoke. I believe that I mentioned in my report that one time Izetbegovic lost his nerve and he said that if he had --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let me --

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: -- if he were trusted the Bosniak army would already have won --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You have again digressed from my question and what you have said is already in your statement, so let's not waste time in this way. Let us move to page 7 in the English and page 15 in the B/C/S. We need to look at the upper part of the English and -- it's actually you speaking and in the context of the arrest of the academic Leovac, you say the following: "To be frank, the more cases like this we have" --

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't have that on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: That's -- it should be -- it should be on page 15 in the B/C/S. That's -- you are speaking. It should be. It's the -- oh, no, it's the previous -- in the B/C/S it's the previous. 31221. Yes. That's where you are speaking in the context of the arrest of academic Leovac. You say: "To be frank, the more cases like this we have, the more we would indirectly tolerate this, signing up to the anarchy that is happening on the other side where the crimes are of course incomparably worse, genocide, et cetera. However, this does not excuse us anything in establishing the rule of law in areas we control." When you speak here of the "other side," that means the Bosnian Serb forces; right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: That's right. However, when I say this I only quote what Izetbegovic and other members of the Presidency belonging to the Muslim and Serbian side said about the Serbian side at the Presidency sessions. I warned them when I heard there was that that was also happening on my side before my own two eyes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we move on to page 10, upper part in the English, and in the B/C/S it should be page 17.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And Mr. Pejanovic is speaking and he says: "I think we are reacting inadequately to the spreading and increase in the number of camps for Muslims in the republic. We are not doing enough to animate the public either in Bosnia or internationally ..." Dr. Kecmanovic, you got information in the Presidency of the many camps for Muslims run by the Serb forces as Mr. Pejanovic says here, and he's speaking about civilians; right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: You should ask Pejanovic that. As far as I can see, I didn't say anything about camps for Muslims. He is the one whose words you are quoting. We heard about that. It was constantly mentioned, but that was propaganda and nobody could be certain of any information that was launched from the other side including this particular information.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can this please be admitted, Your Honour, the entire session -- minutes? This block.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6356, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we please have 65 ter 25020 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And as it is coming up, it is another Presidency session, the 117th of the 12th of June, 1992. And can we please have page 3 in both languages. And now we have here under item 1 and 2 we have Dr. Brkic speaking, the assistant minister of national defence, pointing to the great problem regarding the arrested civilians who are being taken to Pale and other camps. So now it's Mr. Brkic referring to arrested civilians taken to Pale and about other camps. Dr. Kecmanovic, what is he particular referring to? Which civilians were taken to Pale, do you know?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know. No, no. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can this be admitted, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6357, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we please have 65 ter 25056A on the screen, and it is another Presidency session. It's the 114th Session from 9 June, 1992. And page 1 in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We have Commander Halilovic speaking right in the beginning about the military situation and speaking about the artillery fire which was opened at the city during the last 70 hours and he provides further details. As you, yourself, were living in the city, were you in fact a victim of this artillery fire? You experienced it?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I was not a victim. I just testified to that fire, I bore witness to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. And the citizens in Sarajevo were terrified when that happened, were they not?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Including me personally.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you feared -- you yourself and the other citizens, you feared for their lives; right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There is a remark here; however, after very short experience we sought shelter and if we did it in time, if we found shelter in a cellar, in a basement, the danger would be reduced to a minimum because the power of those shells was not so destructive. They could not pierce the walls of a building. You were in danger if you found yourself on the street.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And a little bit further down in this session he also speaks in this -- on this page he speaks -- Halilovic speaks about the lack of artillery on the side of the government forces and he speaks about ten weapons against the 150 on the other side. This lack of weapons on the side of the Bosnian army, that was a concern and a matter of discussion in various Presidency sessions; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And can this please be admitted, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I would like to mention that the ambitions of the BiH army were not to defend the territories that they held, but rather to liberate every single foot of the soil of Bosnia and Herzegovina according to Halilovic. That's why they needed so much weaponry because they had VRS on the one side and Croatian troops on the other in the HVO and the HV.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we please have 65 ter 25087 again on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And it's the Kvocka report that we have spoken before. And I would like to have page -- e-court page 31 on the screen. And I'm sorry, we don't have the B/C/S, so I read slowly that you can follow. You refer here -- is this -- yes. You refer here to the Sarajevo citizens that "became tragic victims of two nationalist extremes ...," you refer to the genocidal and chauvinist hatred. And then you say: "The superior Serbian artillery laid waste to the central and old part of the city, while the Muslim, which grew stronger with time, responded by targeting the newly built residential areas on the outskirts of the city ..." And at the end of the paragraph you refer to the fact that "the quantities of weapons that started arriving was not enough for the Muslim army to threatened the Serbian artillery emplacements positioned on the hills around the edge of the city. Dr. Kecmanovic, that is how you experienced the situation; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. My impression was that there is a disbalance between the two capacities at the moment when I experienced that. We're talking about the period while I was in Sarajevo in practical terms. It was up to the 5th of July, I was in Sarajevo until then, and on the 5th of July I left.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, can this page also be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll add this page to the Exhibit P6351.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And now I want to put the last document to you, and that's 65 ter 25077. And as it is coming up, it is an interview you gave to "Borba," that's a Belgrade newspaper; right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And it's interview on 29th and 30th August 1992. Now we have to move a bit around in the various columns here. On page 1 in the English, the right column, right in the middle, and in the B/C/S, the first page, left column at the end, in relation to the Serbs in Sarajevo you say the following. "The Serbs were in a ... difficult position. On one hand, they shared the same ordeals of war time Sarajevo as the Muslims and Croats, and they were equal victims of the constant artillery and infantry clashes. On the other hand, the situation was made even more difficult for the Serbs by the fact that the war propaganda imposed on an indirect, collective feeling of guilt upon them." And, Dr. Kecmanovic, a few lines further down you also refer to the fact that the members of the other two peoples gradually started to see all Serbs as all the same butchers. What you say here is a fair assessment of the situation at that time; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: What is your question? Just a while ago I said -- I'll try and answer. A few minutes ago in my response I said that I was one of those who feared the shells that were launched from the Serbian side. Nobody targeted either Muslims or Croats. Serbs faced the same threat as the other two peoples. And then it is stated that the Serbs suffered from the predominantly Muslim authorities and at the hand of Muslim civilians because they treated them as collaborators, as those who stayed behind in order to help the Serbian side.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: That's understood. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we please move on to page 4 in the English, left column at the bottom, last paragraph, under the header "Everyone to his own Crowd." And in the B/C/S it's page 2, the left column.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Dr. Kecmanovic, you refer in this paragraph to destruction and expulsion, and at the end you speak about the practical problem that many houses that have been abandoned and burned and property had been stolen and destroyed and so many people, even if they wanted to return, would not have anywhere or anything to go back to. Dr. Kecmanovic, what you describe here, that's the result of the policy that is very often referred to as ethnic cleansing; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: We are coming back to the ambiguity as regards ethnic cleansing, and with the help of the President of the Trial Chamber we managed to establish that that phenomenon which can be termed that way or perhaps in a more adequate way is less stigmatised. That's something that happened on all the three sides. When you quote my words, when I said about the looting of houses and other premises, that was something that somebody from the other side of the front line couldn't do. That could be done only by the people in the city itself. The looting was carried out by the Green Berets, the Patriotic League, and other Muslim paramilitaries, and different structures within the armed forces which -- I apologise, let me finish --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: -- please let me --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Actually, we have very little time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let him finish.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Which carried out those acts. In my report I didn't mention that the entire city, all of its shops were looted. Shop windows were shattered and all that was done by the insiders, the forces who lived inside the city. They started as the Patriotic League and then they were incorporated into the regular BiH forces. That was not done by the Serbs, I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we please move on to the next page in the English and it's the right column, first paragraph. And in the B/C/S we stay with the same page but you have to look at the second column from the left and a bit below the header "quartermaster support."

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Dr. Kecmanovic, you state here the following: "The Muslims really are the most poorly armed and which is particularly tragic they have suffered the most in the war so far ..." Dr. Kecmanovic, you're speaking here in April -- in August 1992 and this is what you wrote; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I was a victim of propaganda here. We received information that during the first several months of war, 300.000 people had been killed in the civil war in Bosnia and that those people were all Muslims. It was later on a few years later that we learned from an independent international commission headed by a Bosniak, Mr. Tokaca, and that commission that there were only a 100.000 victims throughout the war. When I say "only," I sound cynical but that is not my intention. And the break-down of the victims, applying a rational criterion: If you look at it in relative terms with regard to the number of the population, I would say that the number of the victims on all the three sides was proportionally equal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you see -- I can't locate the passage. Where can I find it?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The passage is under the header "Quartermaster Support." It's on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you take a look at the monitor, e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It was supposed to be page 4 in the English -- page 5 in the English, the right -- the right column. Page 5 -- page 3? Page 3 in the English. I was just told page 3 in the English. There should be a header "Quartermaster Support." No, it's actually the next page. It should be the next page -- no, no, no, it's -- it's page -- it's page 3, right column, first paragraph, but it's -- no, it can't be. It's under the quartermaster support. Can we look at the next page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I see a passage which says: "The Muslims really are the most poorly armed" --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: " -- and which is particularly tragic, they have suffered the most in the war so far ..."

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, that's the one. Yes, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: E-court page 4 on the top of the right column.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it the witness read --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- the proper column.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Proper part. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And one last thing, and we remain on the -- the English remains on this page but it has to be a bit lower down. We have to see the -- yes, we have to see this. And for the B/C/S, Dr. Kecmanovic, we have to go back to the first page and you have to look in this little box at the bottom, and it's all under the header "aggressors and 'aggressors.'" The journalist asks about the Serbs and how can one justify the fact that they have used weapons to conquer more than two-thirds of the territory in spite of the fact that they only have one-third of the population in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And you answer, inter alia: "Just as in parliamentary competition, that is, in the political phase, the Muslims and Croats did not shrink from abusing their numerical superiority to out-vote the Serbian side, the Serbian side did not shrink from using the advantage in heavy weapons in war time ..." And you further state: "Everyone in postelection Bosnia-Herzegovina, both in peace and in war, had ruthlessly exploited their advantages without concern for the weaker side ..." Dr. Kecmanovic, that is what you answered at that time. Is it your evidence that the out-voting of a minority by the majority in a parliament can be compared to the ruthless use of heavy weapons and military superiority in achieving one's goals? Do you equal that?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: No. They cannot be equalled because the former was the cause and the latter a consequence. You see, the Muslim side with the assistance of Croatia caused the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina by dominating in the common bodies and abusing the majority, and that's what led to the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina and to everything else. Of course in this context the answer would be the one that you would like; however, I think that the former is worse because of the sequence of events and because of the causality. Of course, in any other situation it would be different.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would like to tender this exhibit, Your Honours, and I see my time is up and that was my last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6359, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Excellency. I will do my best to be fast, but I do believe that we need to release the other witness. We do have only half an hour left, don't we.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dr. Kecmanovic, though, I'd rather address you as "professor," just with the last document we were looking at, can we have the last page. What were the reasons why you got into the Presidency at a time when Biljana and Nikola withdrew?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I personally thought that it was a mistake that Biljana Plavsic and the late Nikola Koljevic left the Presidency. It was along those lines that I spoke to Momcilo Krajisnik at Lukavica when I asked for a meeting with Pejanovic concerning our membership of the Presidency. I thought it would have been much better if they had stayed on. I told them that they should go back to the Presidency, this was still possible, but unless they would do that Pejanovic and I would go into the Presidency because in a way we would be representing the Serbs who were outside of the boundaries of Republika Srpska who were in a way unprotected and the Serbs in Sarajevo directly asked for that because they didn't have any deputies, any government members, or Presidency members who would represent the Serb people. It was my position or rather the condition that I expressed was that all the decisions should be taken by consensus and that there should be the right of veto in the parliament and that this would be able to counter the developments in Sarajevo. I thought that our requests would be agreed to; however, as you can see in the report that I wrote, none of this in fact happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you able to bring about the protection of the Serbs in Sarajevo and were you able to have a bearing on the way the decisions were made in the Presidency in a satisfactory manner?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I have page 1, please. Paragraph 6. [In English] "What was controversial." [Interpretation] "What was controversial." Can we have the left column enlarged, please, in Serbian. Can we scroll down, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How does it start?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we scroll up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "What was controversial."

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what is the meaning of the paragraph. In English it starts with "what was controversial," the second from the bottom, "what was controversial - I do not know how much ...," et cetera. In other words, did you agree that Izetbegovic should promote you to the rank of a representative of all Serbs and not just the Serbs in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I did not accept that I should represent all the Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina, but rather only those who were in that other area which was under the control of the Presidency of Sarajevo. Even in my contacts with official dignitaries such as the visit to Sarajevo of Lord Carrington and Cutileiro when the Presidency prepared the concept of the meeting in advance so that members of the Presidency who included representatives of all the three ethnicities, would, in fact, exclude from negotiations the leadership of Republika Srpska and perhaps even the Croatian leadership which was represented by Stjepan Kljuic in Sarajevo. My response to that was that this would not work. I said that I simply did not represent all the Serbs but only the Serbs in that particular area. If they wanted to communicate with the person who based on the elections represented the majority of the Serbs, I told them that they should go to Pale and talk to you, to Dr. Karadzic, who was the president of Republika Srpska and president of the Serb Democratic Party. Later on at the press conference Lord Carrington did, in fact, say that this was my position and I suppose that you did hear of it at Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This is my next question: Were you able to assist the Serbs in Sarajevo to the extent that you felt was sufficient and were you able to bring your influence to bear on the Presidency to the extent that you found satisfactory?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: If I had been able to, I would probably have remained in Sarajevo. Unfortunately, soon it became all too obvious that nothing will come out of it. Izetbegovic and the Bosniak majority in the Presidency simply had the majority vote and they worked in such a way that they bypassed the Presidency. And whenever I expressed my disagreement with certain issues at the Presidency, they would take it off the agenda and deal with these issues at certain Presidency meetings where I wasn't present. To put it simply, I could not wield any sort of influence. As for specific assistance to the Serbs, in a number of cases, I believe that I was able to provide significant significance by making sure that certain people were released from prisons like Dr. Trifko Guzina [phoen], who was a professor at College of Medicine; and another, Professor Lipovac, who was a professor at the Faculty of Philosophy. They were members of the Political Council of the SDS but they were not members of the SDS, and they were prominent intellectuals. They were detained, their families intervened with me, and I contacted the minister of the interior --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- who told me that he was not aware of this whole system of private prisons and paramilitary groups. Truth be told, he did refer me to one of these paramilitary commands or commanders, one of whom was a criminal from before the war who I knew. And it was actually through him that I was able to get my hands on the important information which did not have to do with only these two individuals but also Professor Leovac's wife who was a professor at the University of Technology, a technological university. They were not the only cases, but these cases involved well-known figures. So this was something that I didn't do as a member of the Presidency or within the line of hierarchy of the Ministry of the Interior; rather, I relied on my personal acquaintances and connections with people who I stayed in contact with after having been in touch with them at a certain point in my earlier career.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the accused repeat the reference and his question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We were able to see from Exhibit P6355, which is a record of the meeting of the Presidency session held on the 6th of June, 1992, when the war was declared in Montenegro and Serbia that neither you nor Mr. Pejanovic were present. What was the view that you and Mr. Pejanovic held vis-a-vis the declaration of war?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Since this topic came up at one of the earlier sessions or it may have been on the same day that the decision was taken at the morning session, when we heard such a decision announced we expressed our reservations and said that we would veto it. However, it was precisely because of that that late at night we would normally work until 6.00 or 7.00 p.m., late in the evening at around midnight an emergency session was called to which neither Mr. Pejanovic or I were invited where this decision was taken. When on the following morning Fikret Abdic announced at a press conference that the decision had been taken, some of the journalists who were there knew that we would not support the decision. They asked Abdic if the decision had been taken unanimously. He said that all those present cast their vote and the Serb representatives weren't there at all in fact.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now call up 19832, 65 ter document. 19832. I don't have a Serbian version, although there might be one in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But I will read it out for you and it will be interpreted -- oh, there is, after all, a copy. We're interested in the beginning. "The latest findings of UNPROFOR about the reasons -- [In English] the reasons for and the perpetrators (Muslims) of the monstrous crime in the bread queue in Sarajevo is reason enough that I can no longer remain a member of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina Nenad Kecmanovic told ..." And the sixth paragraph there you said: "These changes eliminated the minimum conditions under which I entered the Presidency so that now my engagement justifies the simulated civic option behind which Alija Izetbegovic, as one of the national leaders, is trying to impose a unitary solution on less numerous nations, Kecmanovic said." Is that a view you hold today as well?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, today even more than at the time. The course of the later events in Bosnia-Herzegovina through to this day has shown that this is how things stand. Everything that happened later proved my view to be true rather than the other way around. The Bosniak leadership, despite the fact that they formally espoused a civic option, although they could hardly conceal their unitarist pretensions, and this was something that turned out in the later events as well. Nowhere where the Bosniaks were in the majority and wherever they had an opportunity to implement the principles of civic democracy regardless of the Serbs or the Croats, nowhere did they do this, not even in the capital. They had an opportunity to declare it a district based on the proposals from the international community, but they refused to do so and which led to a situation where the Serbs are next to none in Sarajevo. Some people say that there is even more Chinese than Serbs in Sarajevo. Also on the issue of the cantons, they didn't achieve this.
